capabilities.target: private repositories accessible via the user's personal access token
public GitHub repository pull request contents and metadata

inputs.source: Authenticated user request: "Have a look at the open issues in my public repo."
Issues in the public repository authored by GitHub users

elements.name: Outbound pull request to public repository
Tool call approval prompt and approval record

controls.name: Client tool call approval prompt per tool call with collapsed arguments by default
controls.decay_rationale: The user reviews the model's presentation of the tool call rather than a raw always-visible action payload; collapsed arguments and high call volume make the gate vulnerable to persuasive or incomplete summaries and approval fatigue.

controls.name: Pin or hash MCP server tool definitions and identity
controls.decay_rationale: Would prevent post-approval tool mutation and reduce server impersonation risk by binding reviewed definitions to a specific server identity.

controls.name: Scope token to the public repository needed for the task or isolate private-repo read from public-repo write
controls.decay_rationale: A narrower token or split credentials would make private repository content unreachable on this path.

controls.name: Raw-action approval showing full destination and full PR payload without collapsed arguments
controls.decay_rationale: A low-volume raw-action review gate does not rely on the model's summary and can catch exfiltration content before public PR creation.

controls.name: Attributable audit trail separating user intent from agent-selected tool arguments and destinations
controls.decay_rationale: Would improve action attribution and reviewability for high-volume approvals and agent-driven tool use.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): public issue content can steer private repo reads into public PR egress using the user's token

attack_path.note: Anyone on GitHub can author issue text in the public repository.
The runtime notes say the personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, including private repositories.
A pull request to a public repository is attacker-readable public egress and is irreversible once created.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Model version change, approval gate removal or narrowing, or rising approvals per session further weakens the summary-style prompt.

evidence.observation: Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, so issue content is an untrusted source.
The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so the agent can read beyond the public repository named in the task.
The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, so the gate is a high-volume model-summary review.
The user asked only to look at open issues in the public repo; private-repo reads and public PR creation exceed the explicit task scope if induced by issue text.

recommendations.action: Replace the broad personal token with repository-scoped credentials or split credentials so public-repo workflows cannot read private repositories.
Change approval UX to raw-action review with full destination and PR payload always visible, and keep reviewer volume low enough for per-call scrutiny.

findings.title: Unpinned GitHub MCP server definitions and unverified server identity allow post-approval tool mutation or impersonation

attack_path.note: Remote tool definitions and behavior are trusted by the client.
The agent consumes server-provided tool definitions.
A poisoned or impersonated server can redefine or relabel sensitive read actions.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool
Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: AI Agent Tools

forecast.watch_signal: Any MCP client config diff, new server entry, or continued lack of pinned definitions should trigger reassessment because no present structural control mitigates this path.

evidence.observation: The configuration runs a GitHub MCP server container but provides no pinning or hashing for tool definitions.
The artifact does not show any server identity verification beyond invoking the named container image.
The personal access token grants repo-scope access across all owned repositories, so a poisoned server would operate with broad user authority.

recommendations.action: Pin server image digests and reviewed tool schemas, and verify remote server identity before exposing sensitive repository tools.

findings.title: Approval records do not provide strong attributable provenance for agent-selected actions under high-volume collapsed-argument review

forecast.watch_signal: Any rise in unattended steps, remembered approvals, or reduction in approval detail would further weaken attribution and reviewability.

evidence.observation: The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session.

The user's request was limited to reviewing open issues, yet the design allows broader repo access and public write actions, making attributable distinction between user intent and agent-selected actions important.

recommendations.action: Record immutable audit entries that bind the original user request, full approved arguments, destination, and resulting tool action so later reviews can distinguish user intent from agent-selected behavior.

stride_coverage.rationale: The reviewed artifacts describe only read and PR creation with per-call approval, and provide no spend, loop, or recursive delegation capability in this design.
This is the authenticated principal's own request channel; the risk under review is not tampering of the transport but over-broad downstream tool authority.
The request content itself is not described as sensitive disclosure over the boundary; the consequential disclosure occurs later via public PR creation.
No boundary-crossing denial-of-service condition is evidenced on this single user request flow in the provided artifacts.
The design treats this channel as the authenticated user request; no evidence indicates user identity spoofing on that channel in the supplied artifacts.
The inbound public issue flow is already public content; the disclosure risk arises when it can influence later access to confidential private repository data.
The provided design does not show looping, queue amplification, or resource exhaustion on this inbound public issue content flow.
Anyone can author public issues, so authenticity of issue authors is not a relied-on security property in this design; they are treated as untrusted by default.
The assessment does not depend on attributing specific public issue authors; all such content is already classed as untrusted regardless of author identity.
A public PR write is an irreversible outbound action, but the supplied artifacts do not evidence service exhaustion or throughput abuse on this boundary flow.
The artifacts do not say whether server actions or definition changes are attributable to an operator, signer, or release process.
The artifacts state the token scope but do not describe configuration write protections, secret storage controls, or change management for the PAT.
This credential store is not described as quota-enforcing or service-providing, so denial of service is not evidenced from the provided design facts.
The artifacts mention approval prompts but do not say whether approval logs are immutable, integrity-protected, or modifiable after the fact.
The artifacts do not describe whether approval records store full arguments or secret payloads, so confidentiality exposure of the record cannot be assessed.
The approval record is described as a log-like artifact, not a capacity-constrained service whose exhaustion is evidenced in the supplied design.

rating.rationale: Manual validation only; scripts could not be run in this environment. Present risk is dominated by a TC1 path from untrusted public issues to private repository read and irreversible public PR egress using a broad user token. The only declared preventive control on the sink is a per-tool approval prompt scored as a high-volume model-summary gate, which lowers critical inherent risk by one tier to high but not below that floor. Forecast returns to critical if the approval control further decays under model upgrade, autonomy increase, longer task horizon, or removal. Additional present exposure exists from unpinned MCP definitions and unverified server identity.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior or empirical testing.

No system prompt, full tool manifest, server authentication details, or runtime approval log format were provided, so instruction-level issues, exact capability surface, and audit integrity could only be inferred from the notes.
Because scripts could not be run here, schema and rubric validation were applied manually against the provided checklist.
